source.title: SGD: The Role of Implicit Regularization, Batch-size and Multiple-epochs
source.authors: Satyen Kale; Ayush Sekhari; Karthik Sridharan

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical comparisons of SGD, full-batch GD, and multi-pass SGD on constructed stochastic convex optimization problems, measuring population excess risk rather than the image or language benchmark generalization gaps in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's results bear on V5 through theoretical comparisons of full-batch GD with SGD and multi-pass with single-pass SGD. Results cited from other work are not extracted as rows. The two-layer network result compares SGD with ERM on a constructed distribution; it does not test memorization of random labels or natural-label generalization as stated in V1.
record.test_reason: The study proves separations on constructed stochastic optimization problems. It does not test any stated version. In particular, V5 concerns image classifiers or language models with fixed epoch budgets; the GD–SGD theorem concerns population excess-risk rates for arbitrary iteration counts, and the multi-pass comparison changes training duration while keeping batch size one.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusions: constructed problems separate SGD from GD and from RERM with any prescribed sample-independent regularizer, and a validation-selected multi-pass variant retains a single-pass-order guarantee while sometimes improving it. The neural-network implications are exploratory. One qualification is needed: although the main text describes ERM as failing, Appendix F.2 establishes the existence of a bad ERM solution, not failure of every ERM selection rule.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses theoretical constructions and excess-risk bounds, rather than empirical image or language training with controlled epoch budgets.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper's results vary with the constructed problem and training procedure: full-batch GD versus single-pass SGD, and single-pass versus k-pass SGD.

fits_no_version.finding: A constructed population-convex optimization problem separates single-pass SGD's O(n^(-1/2)) excess-risk guarantee from full-batch GD's worse lower bound, irrespective of iteration count and step size as stated in Theorem 3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Full-batch GD can have worse population excess-risk sample complexity than single-pass SGD on constructed stochastic optimization problems.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation-selected multi-pass SGD has a worst-case guarantee close to single-pass SGD and can achieve a better excess-risk rate on a specially constructed problem.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional passes of batch-one SGD can improve population excess risk on some constructed SCO problems.

fits_no_version.finding: For a prescribed sample-independent regularizer, a constructed SCO instance gives RERM constant excess risk while SGD learns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: No sample-independent regularizer makes RERM match SGD uniformly across the studied population-convex optimization problems.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix F.2 constructs a two-layer diagonal ReLU network with an ERM solution having zero empirical loss and population excess risk 1/4, while projected SGD receives a diminishing-risk guarantee.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On a constructed distribution, the existence of an empirical-risk minimizer does not guarantee that every such minimizer generalizes well.

record.problems: Evidence for the mapped version is theoretical and comes from specially constructed SCO problems; the paper does not report empirical benchmark results for large batches or multi-epoch training. The authors state that their constructions are unlike practical neural networks.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible result rows omitted. The paper's theorem that RERM has an Ω(1) lower bound on the same constructed problem is retained as R5, though it is an adjacent comparison rather than a direct batch-size result.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy using the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width needed to fit.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning regimes.
Large-batch penalties in image classifiers or language models under fixed epoch budgets, and their recovery through recipe changes or longer training.
Dropout's effect on held-out classification error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Accuracy after removing memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Theoretical evidence is eligible in principle; the exclusion here follows from the mismatch with the stated versions. Neither the absence of benchmark experiments nor untested recipe adaptations warrants a limits_scope verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization alongside natural-label generalization; the paper does not test arbitrary-label fit or held-out accuracy on natural labels.
No network-width sweep or test-error measurement around or beyond the width needed to fit the training data.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected image classifiers.

The comparisons use constructed SCO problems and excess-risk guarantees, not image classifiers or language models; they do not test batch sizes beyond a workload-dependent size under fixed epoch budgets, or normalization and regularization changes.
No sharpness, norm, or margin measurement linked to a generalization gap.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: GD on training loss
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical full-batch gradient descent on a constructed SCO instance; lower bound holds for any step size and number of iterations.
rows.baseline: Single-pass SGD with step size 1/√n: O(1/√n)
rows.note: The paper states that this instance gives worse performance for GD (large batch) than SGD; this is a theoretical bound, not a measured benchmark result.
rows.check: Constructed SCO excess risk does not establish V5's fixed-epoch batch-size effect in image or language models. The main theorem states Ω(n^(-5/12)), but Appendix C.4 proves a bound with a log^4(n) denominator; report the logarithmic qualification.

rows.subject: Multi-pass SGD
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical adaptive multi-epoch SGD algorithm, with validation on a held-out half of the sample.
rows.measure: Expected population loss relative to the single-pass SGD output
rows.value: At most the single-pass output's expected loss plus Õ(1/√n)
rows.note: The proposition gives a bound comparing the multi-pass output with single-pass SGD; it does not report an image or language benchmark.
rows.check: This is a guarantee for the authors' validation-selected multi-pass algorithm, not a batch-size comparison. Its additive Õ(n^(-1/2)) allowance does not prove identical population loss. Appendix D.1 assumes bounded losses, and Algorithm 1 adds projection at epoch starts.

rows.subject: Single-pass SGD
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical single-pass SGD on a constructed SCO instance.
rows.value: Lower bound Ω(1/√n); step size 1/√n achieves the stated 1/√n rate
rows.note: The reported bound is for the paper's constructed problem.
rows.check: The single-pass lower bound is a valid theoretical comparator for R4, but it measures neither batch-size variation nor any other claim version.

rows.subject: Multi-pass SGD
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical k-pass multi-pass SGD on the same constructed SCO instance as R3.
rows.note: The theorem states that multi-pass SGD can outperform single-pass SGD on this problem.
rows.check: Both procedures use batch size one; the comparison changes the number of passes. The constructed samples contain k independent components exposed on successive passes. Appendix D.2 qualifies the final validation-selected rate with k=o(n), a condition omitted from the row.

rows.subject: RERM
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical regularized empirical risk minimization on the constructed problem used in Theorem 4.
rows.note: This compares RERM with SGD, not batch sizes; included as an adjacent result on the claim's generalization subject.
rows.check: RERM versus SGD on a constructed SCO problem is outside all eight versions. The construction may depend on the prescribed regularizer; this is not a single instance shown to defeat every regularizer simultaneously.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
